title: Sociological perspectives on artificial intelligence: A typological reading
pub: Sociology Compass, vol. 15, no. 3, e12851 (March 2021 issue; first published online 18 February 2021), DOI 10.1111/soc4.12851
author: Zheng Liu

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source presents competing employment accounts rather than adopting a clear position on the cluster’s legal-workflow proposition. Its discussion of differential task vulnerability, tacit knowledge, worker agency and critiques of deterministic displacement is broadly compatible with task reconfiguration over wholesale replacement, but it does not directly assess legal workflows, verification, productivity gains or competence risks.
qs: Some bleak observations have been made (Brynjolfsson & McAfee, 2014; for a helpful review, see; Wajcman, 2017), including predictions such as that up to 47% of today's jobs will be replaced by AI (Frey & Osborne, 2013).

Some criticise that owing to their epistemological flaw of technological determinism, the pessimistic accounts fail to take into account the political‐economic and socio‐cultural complexity of automation's impact on the workplace and that their conclusions are therefore one‐sided and untenable (Boyd & Holton, 2017; Clark & Gevorkyan, 2020; Spencer, 2017).

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The supplied excerpts are bibliography-only and provide no substantive claims, evidence, reasoning or recommendations attributable to the source. Citation of relevant literature alone cannot establish whether the source supports, extends, redirects or opposes the cluster’s account of AI redistributing legal tasks, status and professional power.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Liu supports the cluster’s rejection of technologically determined substitution by showing that AI operates within sociotechnical systems and that employment effects depend on political-economic, sociocultural and tacit-knowledge factors. The source materially extends the cluster’s work-redesign framing by adding that institutional values, power and social learning shape both system performance and deployment outcomes, although it does not provide legal-task evidence or address verification directly.
qs: By demonstrating that fundamentally determining the workings of HFT is “the interaction of people, organizations, algorithms, and machines”, rather than some “black box” technology, Mackenzie highlights the social embeddedness of new technologies including AI.

Some criticise that owing to their epistemological flaw of technological determinism, the pessimistic accounts fail to take into account the political‐economic and socio‐cultural complexity of automation's impact on the workplace and that their conclusions are therefore one‐sided and untenable (Boyd & Holton, 2017; Clark & Gevorkyan, 2020; Spencer, 2017).

st.t: Worker power: Automation outcomes depend on consultation
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s contingent, non-technologically deterministic account by arguing that workplace effects depend on political-economic and socio-cultural context and by recognising worker agency. It does not materially address consultation, surveillance or contestability, so its support is partial rather than an extension of the cluster’s governance claims.
qs: Some criticise that owing to their epistemological flaw of technological determinism, the pessimistic accounts fail to take into account the political‐economic and socio‐cultural complexity of automation's impact on the workplace and that their conclusions are therefore one‐sided and untenable (Boyd & Holton, 2017; Clark & Gevorkyan, 2020; Spencer, 2017).
McClure (2018) explores how workers' agency affects their job security in the age of robotics and AI.

kp.k: Three analytic perspectives organise sociological research on AI
kp.d: Liu proposes a typology distinguishing AI as science or a scientific research field, AI as a metatechnology comprising applications and subtechnologies, and AI development as a social phenomenon. This is a cross-domain conceptual review, not a study of restructuring in legal services.
qs: The “scientific AI” analytic perspective focuses on the core scientific features of AI as a science or a scientific research field.
The “technical AI” analytic perspective treats AI as a metatechnology and analyses the social ramifications of various AI applications and subtechnologies.

Instead, it (a) views AI development as a social phenomenon; (b) takes this phenomenon as its object of study; and (c) analyses its interactions with the wider social, cultural, economic and political conditions in which it occurs and by which it is affected.

kp.k: The review identifies strands rather than exhaustively surveying evidence
kp.d: Liu identifies literature through searches of Google Scholar, Web of Science and Scopus, followed by reference tracing. The review selectively discusses principal research strands and foundational work from the 1980s and 1990s, rather than providing a comprehensive survey.
qs: Since the size of the literature is beyond the capacity of a review paper, I focus my attention on identifying the main research strands and discussing the key work in the literature, rather than offering a comprehensive survey of it.

kp.k: Historical shifts do not make the typology chronological
kp.d: Liu connects scientific AI research particularly with the 1980s and 1990s, technical AI research with commercialisation in the 2000s and 2010s, and cultural AI research with growing social embeddedness. These are overlapping analytic perspectives, not successive stages that displace earlier approaches, and other conceptions remain possible.
qs: The distinction between the three perspectives is analytic rather than temporal.
There is no reason why “AI” cannot be conceptualised and examined in other senses and from other perspectives

kp.k: Research agendas reflect social beliefs and resource struggles
kp.d: Liu reports Bloomfield's argument that socially constituted thought styles shaped postwar US AI research, and Fleck's account of powerful researchers controlling directions and appointments while competing with established disciplines for funding. Liu recommends renewed attention to corporate influence over AI research and resistance within the AI community.
qs: Bloomfield examines AI development in the US after World War II and illustrates that the direction and outcomes of AI research during this period were shaped by three dominant “thought styles”, namely, expectation of imminent breakthroughs, faith in the universality of computer programs and technological determinism.
However, outside the AI field, their authority would be eclipsed by researchers in more established disciplines, such as computer science and mathematics, when bidding for research funding.

kp.k: AI systems reproduce developers' values and assumptions
kp.d: Liu presents Forsythe's 1993 research as foundational evidence that developers embed existing cultural assumptions in AI systems. Relating this to later research on discriminatory outputs, Liu stresses the persistence of problems identified almost three decades earlier rather than treating bias as a newly discovered issue.
qs: She maintains that, wittingly or unwittingly, AI developers bring pre‐existing values, beliefs and assumptions into what they design.
AI systems are therefore anything but objective and value free.
Why do these problems, exposed nearly 3 decades ago, still persist today?

kp.k: AI can constitute social relations and transform institutions
kp.d: Liu reviews arguments that AI is not merely socially produced but can itself assume social roles and shape institutions. Woolgar's proposed sociology of machines challenges an intrinsic human–machine distinction in social capacities, while Bloomfield recommends using social-science and humanities insights to improve machine knowledge production.
qs: For some sociologists, AI is not only a socially constituted enterprise, but also socially constituting in the sense that when implemented in a social environment an AI system can assume social roles, enact social practices and form social relations.

Bloomfield suggests that AI developers can better their systems' ability to generate knowledge by assimilating social science and humanities research on the nature of knowledge and the process of knowledge production.

kp.k: Contextual understanding challenges claims of human-like machine intelligence
kp.d: Liu reports Collins's argument that mechanical capabilities such as pattern identification do not establish genuine human intelligence because machines lack contextual understanding. Suchman's related argument emphasises situated human action rather than mechanically executing prescribed programs. These are attributed theoretical positions, not performance measurements produced by this review.
qs: they lack the ability to “see” and “understand” contexts, a core quality of human intelligence.

Suchman (1987, 2007, 2011) rejects the idea that robots can be programmed to behave like humans, on the grounds that whereas humans “study” social settings before acting, robots “act” mechanically as a result of prescribed programs.

kp.k: Employment forecasts are contested by socially situated accounts
kp.d: Liu reports the prediction attributed to Frey and Osborne (2013) that up to 47% of jobs would be replaced by AI, but contrasts it with sociologists' criticism of technological determinism. The review presents political-economic and sociocultural conditions as necessary considerations, rather than endorsing that replacement forecast.
qs: including predictions such as that up to 47% of today's jobs will be replaced by AI (Frey & Osborne, 2013).
Many sociologists, however, have drawn different conclusions.
the pessimistic accounts fail to take into account the political‐economic and socio‐cultural complexity of automation's impact on the workplace

kp.k: Tacit knowledge and worker agency condition employment effects
kp.d: Liu reports Pettersen's 2019 argument that AI will not threaten complex knowledge workers because it cannot deploy experts' tacit knowledge. Liu also recounts McClure's 2018 suggestion that positive attitudes toward AI support adaptation, employability and job security, whereas fear inhibits learning. These remain the cited researchers' claims, not legal-profession findings or new causal estimates.
qs: AI will not threaten human “knowledge workers”, for it lacks the human expert's ability to deploy tacit knowledge to assess and resolve problems.

He suggests that workers with a more positive attitude towards AI tend to have higher job security and increased employability because they are more willing to embrace and adapt to the new AI‐present workplace order.

kp.k: Autonomous driving requires social learning alongside technical improvement
kp.d: Liu presents Stilgoe's governance argument and Marres's design-and-experimentation argument that autonomous vehicles require attention to social deficiencies, risks and participation. Liu separately characterises Bissell and colleagues' predictions about labour relations, inequality and institutional change as speculative and requiring substantive empirical testing.
qs: requires not only better ML techniques but also better “social learning” on the part of all parties involved in making and governing the technology
such an element of social learning must be incorporated in the design and experimentation phases of the relevant systems.
more substantive research is required to test its wide‐ranging predictions.

kp.k: Automation does not establish autonomous moral decision-making
kp.d: Reviewing military applications, Liu distinguishes execution without external human involvement from rational decision-making situated in social, cultural, historical and ethical contexts. The reviewed literature questions trusting automated systems with targeting and firing and treating them as accountable decision-makers.
qs: A common concern has been to what extent “automated” systems should be trusted to make high‐stake decisions such as targeting and firing.
Underlying this concern is a distinction in social science traditions between automation and autonomy.
“autonomy”, and thus to apply them in warfare as though they could be held accountable for their “decisions” would have severe legal, social, political, ethical and moral consequences.

kp.k: Algorithmic trading remains embedded in human institutions
kp.d: Liu uses MacKenzie's studies of high-frequency trading to challenge the appearance of autonomous technology replacing experts. Although systems execute orders without instructions from human traders on individual transactions, their operation depends on material infrastructure, organisations, people and interactions.
qs: HFT uses complex algorithmic computer programs to automatically transact large volumes of orders at very high speeds independently of human traders' instructions on specific orders.
in a complex web not only of symbolic data and algorithms but also of real humans, institutions and their interactions.

kp.k: Automated surveillance creates public benefits and misuse risks
kp.d: Liu reviews recognition and emotion-detection technologies across education, transport and public services. McStay warns that commercial and political actors may exploit these technologies for private interests; the review recommends caution over privacy, transparency and social control.
qs: McStay (2018) warns that these technologies are subject to misuse by commercial and political entities to advance their private interests at the expense of public good.
Together these studies draw attention to the question of how automated surveillance has both benefits and risks for society as a whole and should be managed with caution.

kp.k: Algorithmic decisions can reinforce inequality and concentrated power
kp.d: Liu synthesises work on socially consequential sorting, profiling and decision-making. Eubanks argues that public-service algorithms disadvantage poor people; Noble argues that technically neutral search systems reinforce racism; Bucher describes platforms shaping sociality, emotions and political behaviour. The mechanisms include inherited developer biases and mitigation that is unavailable, ineffective or ignored.
qs: algorithm development is not a neutral process but one that retains and reproduces the values and biases of the developers
mitigating mechanisms are not always technically available or effective, or else are available but are, for various reasons, ignored by the algorithms' users.
these algorithms serve to reinforce racism in society and are therefore morally and politically problematic.

kp.k: AI culture can legitimise alienation and unpaid labour
kp.d: Liu reports Turkle's concern that describing humans through computer metaphors can shape cognition and behaviour, and Berman's Marxist argument that AI narratives legitimate alienating conditions and elite power. Mühlhoff's 2020 analysis adds that deep learning depends on extraction of often involuntary user-generated data and free human labour.
qs: the proliferation of AI can have a colonising effect on human society by causing humans to think and behave like computers.
helps to justify the alienating social and economic conditions in capitalist societies
AI and an AI culture can thereby help to widen and deepen the unequal power relations in society rather than to abate them.
the exploitation of human capacities and free human labour

kp.k: Cultural framing influences AI development and acceptance
kp.d: Liu reviews how academics, industry practitioners and policymakers frame educational AI to advance different agendas; how Japanese roboticists draw on valued cultural traditions to secure acceptance; and how technological myths helped popularise AI between the 1950s and 1970s. Liu recommends active framing and deframing by researchers, users and regulators to influence socially beneficial design.
qs: Their focus is on how different groups leverage different cultural resources and traditions to develop AI narratives that help to advance their differing agendas.
These studies illustrate the importance of effective cultural framing for AI development.
In a sense, cultural framing is a form of social intervention in AI design.

kp.k: Broader sociological inquiry requires analytical depth and collaboration
kp.d: Liu welcomes Elliott's placement of AI within the digital revolution and its implications for identity, economic organisation, interaction, mobility and politics, while criticising descriptive treatment and bold, insufficiently supported claims. Liu recommends collaboration between social scientists and the AI community and a sociology of AI extending beyond sociology of science and STS.
qs: First, the text is more descriptive than analytical.
The AI community and the social scientist must work together if the technology is to be made more socially beneficial and sustainable.
The sociology of AI should contain the sociology of science and STS research on AI, but it should not be limited to that.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Liu reviews AI's effects on work, institutions, inequality and social power; this is a cross-domain sociology source, not a prediction about legal-service markets.
pts.d: Liu's synthesis presents AI as socially shaped and socially consequential rather than an independently determining technological force. On employment, she reports competing positions: substantial replacement predictions versus arguments that tacit knowledge and workplace adaptation protect workers. These are positions in the reviewed literature, not original employment forecasts by Liu. Her discussion of financial trading stresses that automation remains embedded in human and institutional relationships. Her synthesis of algorithm studies identifies risks of discriminatory decisions, reinforcement of inequality and concentrated corporate power. She also discusses surveillance's benefits and risks and the accountability problems of treating automated weapons as autonomous decision-makers. In the cultural analysis, Liu argues that AI development creates benefits and difficult-to-identify social challenges, and that cultural framing can influence its development and acceptance. She makes no concrete claim about law-firm staffing, legal fees, lawyer displacement or legal-service providers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is a selective literature review combining empirical studies, historical accounts and theoretical arguments, not new measurements of AI's effects.
pts.d: Liu describes database searches followed by reference tracing, explicitly limiting the article to major research strands and selected works rather than a comprehensive survey. For employment, she discusses earlier automation research, a replacement prediction attributed to Frey and Osborne (2013), critiques of technological determinism, and work on tacit knowledge and worker attitudes. For institutional effects, she draws on MacKenzie's studies of high-frequency trading; Eubanks on public-service decision systems; Noble on search discrimination; Bucher on platform power; and studies of surveillance. Historical and cultural claims draw on research concerning developers' values, AI narratives, educational AI and Japanese robotics. Liu explicitly distinguishes some broad predictions from empirical findings: she describes the autonomous-driving account by Bissell and colleagues as speculative and requiring further testing. She also criticises Elliott's broader account for insufficient analytical depth. The paper supplies no legal-services dataset, model benchmark or quantified estimate of changes to professional legal work.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes historical and contemporary developments as of 2021; most prospective claims lack a fixed forecast horizon and depend on social context, governance and capabilities.
pts.d: Liu situates the scientific perspective primarily in the 1980s–1990s, the technical perspective in the 2000s–2010s, and growing cultural attention in the contemporary period, while explicitly rejecting a strictly chronological typology. Employment outcomes are presented as conditional on task characteristics, tacit knowledge, worker adaptation and political-economic circumstances. Harm from algorithmic decisions is qualified by deployment in consequential settings without adequate mitigation. Safe and socially appropriate autonomous driving is presented as requiring social learning and governance, not merely technical improvement. Broad predictions about driverless vehicles' effects on labour relations and inequality are flagged as needing substantive empirical testing. The article does not give a dated timetable for these transformations or for changes in legal services.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include workers, disadvantaged public-service users, platform users, people subject to surveillance, AI developers and institutions governing technology.
pts.d: Liu's review distinguishes workers performing mechanical tasks from knowledge workers relying on contextual and tacit expertise; it also discusses differences associated with workers' willingness to adapt. Public-service recipients, especially poor and underprivileged people, are described in the reviewed research as exposed to discriminatory algorithmic decisions. Search and platform users face effects on visibility, social interaction, emotion and political behaviour. Students, transport users and the public are affected by surveillance's implications for privacy, transparency and social control. Human-generated data contributors supply capacities and labour used in AI development. Developers, corporations, academics, policymakers and regulators shape AI through design choices, funding, governance and cultural framing. Sociologists are both the article's intended audience and potential contributors to socially beneficial AI development. These groups should not be recast as legal-market segments: the article does not identify lawyers, law firms or corporate legal departments as a separately analysed population.
